source_text:
Ὅτε γὰρ ἔμελλε
συμβάλλειν τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ Ἡσαὺ κακίας γέμοντι καὶ φονοκτονίας, παρεκάλει
τὸν Θεὸν λέγων, Κύριε, ῥῦσαί με ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ μου Ἡσαὺ, ὅτι φοβοῦμαι αὐτὸν
πάνυ· καὶ ἱκέτευε τὸν Θεὸν, ὡς κατὰ πονηροῦ τὴν εὐχὴν τιθέμενος. Ὅτε δὲ
συνήντησε τῷ ἀδελφῷ, ἠθικότητι καὶ κολακείᾳ τὸν θυμὸν ἡμέρωσε, καὶ τὴν
πονηρίαν ἔσβεσε. Τί γάρ φησι πρὸς τὸν Ἡσαύ; Εἶδόν σου τὸ πρόσωπον, ὡς εἴ τις ἴδοι
πρόσωπον Θεοῦ. Καὶ εἰ μὲν ἔλεγεν ὁ Ἰακὼβ ταῦτα, ἵνα διὰ τῆς ἀπάτης νικήσῃ τὸν
ἀδελφὸν, κακῶς ἐλάλει· εἰ δὲ εἶπεν, ἵνα τὸν φόβον ἐκφύγῃ, καλῶς ἐχρήσατο τῇ
πανουργίᾳ. Γίνεσθε οὖν φρόνιμοι ὡς ὁ ὄφις· μὴ θυμώδεις, μὴ ἰοβόλοι, ἀλλὰ
φρόνιμοι, καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί. Ἔστι δὲ τὴν περιστερὰν καὶ εἰς κακίαν καὶ
εἰς ἀρετὴν ἐκλαβεῖν· καὶ ὅπως, ἄκουε· Ἐὰν ᾖς ἀλόγιστος καὶ ἀδιάκριτος, καὶ κακίας
ἔμπειρος μόνον, διαβάλλει σε ἡ Γραφὴ ὡς ἀσύνετον. Ἐφραῒμ γὰρ, φησὶν, ὡς
περιστερὰ ἄνους, οὐκ ἔχουσα καρδίαν. Ἐὰν οὖν τὸ ἄνουν φυγὼν, τὸ ἀκέραιον
κατορθώσῃς, ἔχεις τὴν σύνεσιν τελείαν, οὐ συμμιγνὺς αὐτῇ λ. αὐτὴν τῇ κακίᾳ· καὶ
ἀκούεις παρὰ τοῦ Κυρίου, Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι ὡς ὁ ὄφις, καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί.
Μὴ τοίνυν ἁπλῶς, ἀδελφὲ, τὰς Γραφὰς ἀναγίνωσκε, καὶ τὰς εἰκόνας εἰς κακίας
ἐκλάμβανε παρ' αὐτῆς, μερίζουσα λ. μεριζούσης τούτῳ μὲν τοῦτο, τούτῳ δὲ ἕτερον.
Θέλεις οὖν μαθεῖν; πρόσεχε ἀκριβῶς τοῖς 56.521 λεγομένοις· Καλεῖ λέοντα ἡ Γραφή·
Σκύμνος γὰρ, φησὶ, λέοντος Ἰούδα· ἐκ βλαστοῦ, υἱέ μου, ἀνέβης· ἀναπεσὼν
ἐκοιμήθης ὡς λέων. Ὧδε τὸ, Ὡς λέων, τὸ ἀνδρεῖον σημαίνει· καὶ γὰρ καὶ περὶ τοῦ
δικαίου τὴν αὐτὴν τίθησιν εἰκόνα· ∆ίκαιος γὰρ, φησὶν, ὡς λέων πέποιθεν. Ἀνδρεῖος
τοίνυν ὁ δίκαιος, οὐκ ἐν τῷ δρᾷν κακῶς, ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ διαπτύειν τὰ παρὰ τῶν πονηρῶν
ἐπαγόμενα. Καλεῖ καὶ τὸν Σωτῆρα λέοντα, διὰ τὸ ἐκ βασιλικῆς εἶναι φυλῆς. Ὥσπερ
γὰρ τῶν τετραπόδων ὑπάρχει βασιλεὺς ὁ λέων, οὕτω καὶ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐβασίλευσεν
ἡ Ἰούδα φυλὴ, ἐξ ἧς ὁ Σωτὴρ ἀνέτειλε. Καὶ μὴ νομίσῃς, ἀγαπητὲ, ἀνάξιον εἶναι τοῦ
Χριστοῦ τὸ εἰκόνι λέοντος ἀπεικάζεσθαι· σχηματίζει γὰρ ἡ Γραφὴ τὴν εἰκόνα ταύτην
καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῆς τῆς Θεότητος. Ἄκουε γοῦν οἷα ὁ προφήτης φησί· Λέων ἐρεύξεται, καὶ
τίς οὐ φοβηθήσεται; Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἐλάλησε, καὶ τίς οὐ προφητεύσει; Κατὰ τὸ
δυνατὸν τοίνυν, καὶ τὸ φοβερὸν, καὶ τὸ βασιλικὸν, λέοντι ἀπεικάζεται ὁ Χριστός.
Καλεῖται δὲ καὶ ὁ διάβολος λέων, οὐχ ὡς δυνατὸς, οὐδ' ὡς φοβερὸς, ἀλλ' ὡς
πλήκτης, ὡς τύραννος, ὡς ἀφανιστικός. Λέγει δὲ περὶ τούτου ὁ μακάριος Πέτρος ὁ
ἀπόστολος· Ἰδοὺ ὁ ἐχθρὸς ὑμῶν διάβολος περιέρχεται, ὡς λέων, ζητῶν καταπιεῖν
ψυχήν. Μέριζε τοίνυν τῶν ἀναγνωσμάτων τὰς θεωρίας, μήποτε ἐναντία δοκοῦντα
τῇ λέξει συγχέῃ σου τὴν διάνοιαν. Εἶπεν ἡ Γραφὴ λέοντα καὶ λέοντα· ἀλλὰ τὸν μὲν
κατὰ τὸ βασιλικὸν καὶ δυνατὸν, τὸν δὲ κατὰ τὸ ἀφανιστικὸν καὶ δηλητήριον.
orientation: The homilist is explaining how Scripture uses the same animal images sometimes for virtue and sometimes for vice, and has just shown Jacob as prudent as a serpent but not venomous.
pass_a_gloss: For when he was about to meet his brother Esau, full of malice and murderous intent, he called upon God, saying, Lord, deliver me from my brother Esau, because I fear him greatly; and he entreated God, as one placing his prayer against an evil man. But when he met his brother, he softened his anger with courtesy and flattery, and quenched his wickedness. For what does he say to Esau? I have seen your face, as if someone saw the face of God. And if Jacob said these things in order to conquer his brother through deceit, he spoke badly; but if he said them in order to escape fear, he used prudence well. Be therefore prudent as the serpent; not wrathful, not venomous, but prudent, and innocent as the doves. And it is possible to take the dove both for vice and for virtue; and how, listen: If you are unreasoning and undiscerning, and experienced only in evil, Scripture accuses you as senseless. For Ephraim, it says, is like a senseless dove, not having a heart. If therefore, having fled the senselessness, you achieve the innocence, you have perfect understanding, not mixing it with evil; and you hear from the Lord, Be prudent as the serpent, and innocent as the doves. Do not therefore, brother, read the Scriptures simply, and take the images for vices from it, when it apportions to this one this, and to that one another. Do you wish then to learn? Attend carefully to the things said: Scripture calls the lion: For a lion's whelp, it says, is Judah; from a shoot, my son, you went up; having lain down, you slept as a lion. Here the 'as a lion' signifies the courageous; for also concerning the righteous man it sets the same image: For the righteous man, it says, trusts as a lion. Courageous therefore is the righteous man, not in doing evil, but in despising the things brought on by the wicked. It calls also the Savior a lion, because he is from a royal tribe. For just as the lion is king of the four-footed animals, so also the tribe of Judah reigned over the Jews, from which the Savior arose. And do not think, beloved, that it is unworthy of Christ to be likened by the image of a lion; for Scripture shapes this image also upon the Godhead itself. Hear then what the prophet says: A lion will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy? According to the powerful, then, and the fearful, and the royal, Christ is likened to a lion. And the devil is also called a lion, not as powerful, nor as fearful, but as a striker, as a tyrant, as a destroyer. And concerning this one the blessed Peter the apostle says: Behold, your enemy the devil goes about, as a lion, seeking to swallow a soul. Divide therefore the contemplations of the readings, lest things seeming contrary in the wording confuse your mind. Scripture said lion and lion; but the one according to the royal and powerful, the other according to the destructive and poisonous.

choices.why: Keeps both nouns distinct; 'courtesy' renders the moral character term, 'flattery' the soothing speech, without softening the potentially negative sense of κολακεία.
The verb σβέννυμι is literally 'to extinguish'; 'quenched' preserves the fire metaphor and the object's force.
Renders the alpha-privative adjective literally as lacking discernment, matching the homilist's contrast with σύνεσις.
The verb means literally 'to spit upon'; 'despise' conveys the contemptuous rejection intended, while remaining natural English.
Renders the agent noun literally as one who strikes, preserving the violent image the homilist applies to the devil.
The adjective means 'destructive' or 'ruinous'; the noun 'destroyer' keeps the agentive force parallel with 'striker' and 'tyrant'.

pass_b_english: For when he was about to meet his brother Esau, who was full of malice and murderous intent, he entreated God, saying, “Lord, rescue me from my brother Esau, for I am very afraid of him” (Genesis 32:11). He begged God, offering his prayer as against an evil man. But when he met his brother, he softened his anger with courtesy and flattery, and quenched his wickedness. What does he say to Esau? “I have seen your face as one sees the face of God” (Genesis 33:10). If Jacob said this to defeat his brother through deceit, he spoke wrongly; but if he said it to escape fear, he used prudence well. So be prudent as the serpent—not hot-tempered, not venomous, but prudent, and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16).

Now the dove can be taken as an image of either vice or virtue. Hear how. If you are thoughtless and undiscerning, and acquainted only with evil, Scripture accuses you as senseless. For it says, “Ephraim is like a senseless dove, without a heart” (Hosea 7:11). If, then, you flee thoughtlessness and achieve innocence, you have perfect understanding, not mixing it with evil. And you hear from the Lord, “Be prudent as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16).

So do not read the Scriptures carelessly, brother, and do not take the images from them as images of vice, when Scripture assigns one meaning to one thing and another meaning to another. Do you want to learn? Pay close attention to what is said. Scripture speaks of a lion: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you went up; lying down, you slept like a lion” (Genesis 49:9). Here “like a lion” signifies courage. For it also applies the same image to the righteous person: “The righteous person is confident like a lion” (Proverbs 28:1). The righteous person, then, is courageous—not in doing evil, but in despising the attacks brought by the wicked.

Scripture also calls the Savior a lion, because he is from a royal tribe. For just as the lion is king of the four-footed animals, so the tribe of Judah ruled over the Jews, and from it the Savior arose. And do not think, beloved, that it is unworthy of Christ to be compared to the image of a lion. For Scripture shapes this image even for the Godhead itself. Hear what the prophet says: “A lion will roar—who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken—who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3:8). So Christ is compared to a lion for power, for fearsomeness, and for royalty.

The devil is also called a lion—not as powerful, nor as fearsome, but as a striker, as a tyrant, as a destroyer. The blessed apostle Peter says about him: “Behold, your enemy the devil prowls around like a lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Distinguish, then, the meanings of the readings, lest things that seem contradictory in the wording confuse your mind. Scripture said “lion” and “lion”—but one according to what is royal and powerful, the other according to what is destructive and deadly.
notes: The source contains two apparent OCR or scribal corruptions marked with λ.: 'οὐ συμμιγνὺς αὐτῇ λ. αὐτὴν τῇ κακίᾳ' and 'μερίζουσα λ. μεριζούσης'. The gloss renders the likely intended sense without inventing text.

problems.quote: So according to what is possible, Christ is compared to a lion for power, for fearfulness, and for royalty.
problems.source_quote: Κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν τοίνυν, καὶ τὸ φοβερὸν, καὶ τὸ βασιλικὸν, λέοντι ἀπεικάζεται ὁ Χριστός.
problems.why: Κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν means 'for power' (the first of three parallel qualities), not 'according to what is possible,' so it is both mistranslated and double-translated.
problems.fix: So Christ is compared to a lion for power, for fearsomeness, and for royalty.
problems.ruling: Κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν parallels φοβερὸν and βασιλικόν as might, not 'the possible'; English misrenders and duplicates power.

edits.old: So according to what is possible, Christ is compared to a lion for power, for fearfulness, and for royalty.
edits.new: So Christ is compared to a lion for power, for fearfulness, and for royalty.

fixed: Fixed mistranslation: Κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν καὶ τὸ φοβερὸν καὶ τὸ βασιλικὸν are three parallel qualities, so removed erroneous 'according to what is possible' that mistranslated δυνατὸν and duplicated 'for power'.

problems.why: In modern English, 'fearfulness' means being afraid or timid, inverting Greek τὸ φοβερόν, which means inspiring awe or fear (echoing Amos 3:8).
problems.ruling: τὸ φοβερὸν is awe-inspiring; 'fearfulness' reads as timidity, inverting Amos 3:8 sense.

problems.why: Applied to a person, 'fearful' in modern English means afraid or timid, whereas φοβερός here means awe-inspiring or fearsome.
problems.ruling: οὐδ' ὡς φοβερὸς denies majestic fearsomeness; 'fearful' suggests timid, misleading the contrast with Christ.

edits.old: for power, for fearfulness, and for royalty
edits.new: for power, for fearsomeness, and for royalty

edits.old: not as powerful, nor as fearful, but as a striker
edits.new: not as powerful, nor as fearsome, but as a striker

fixed: for fearfulness (καὶ τὸ φοβερὸν): fixed to fearsomeness — Greek means inspiring fear, echoing Amos 3:8
nor as fearful (οὐδ' ὡς φοβερὸς): fixed to fearsome — Greek means awe-inspiring, not afraid

problems.quote: the other according to what is destructive and poisonous
problems.source_quote: τὸν δὲ κατὰ τὸ ἀφανιστικὸν καὶ δηλητήριον
problems.why: δηλητήριον here means harmful, deadly, or baneful, not "poisonous," which is an absurd attribute for a lion.
problems.fix: the other according to what is destructive and deadly
problems.ruling: δηλητήριον is deadly/baneful harm, not venom; poisonous misleads on the devil-as-lion contrast.

edits.old: the other according to what is destructive and poisonous
edits.new: the other according to what is destructive and deadly

fixed: Fixed poisonous to deadly: source δηλητήριον means deadly/harmful, not poisonous, absurd for a lion.

last_rejected.quote: he softened his anger with courtesy and flattery
last_rejected.source_quote: ἠθικότητι καὶ κολακείᾳ τὸν θυμὸν ἡμέρωσε
last_rejected.why: “His anger” reads as Jacob’s; Greek tames the brother’s wrath.
last_rejected.fix: he softened Esau’s anger with courtesy and flattery
last_rejected.ruling: In context of Esau's malice, 'his anger' for τὸν θυμὸν clearly means Esau's, since flattery softens another's anger; pronoun wording is stylistic.

last_rejected.why: “His wickedness” suggests Jacob’s; Greek means the malice was put out.
last_rejected.ruling: Active ἔσβεσε takes τὴν πονηρίαν (Esau's malice, matching πονηροῦ); context makes the referent clear, so 'his wickedness' is a stylistic choice.
